newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer welcomes stability pact, waits for use.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer welcomes stability pact, waits for use.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday welcomed European nations' backing of a stable currency union but said their commitment still needed to be demonstrated by sticking to an agreed stability pact.

Nearly one week after European Union leaders at the Dublin summit accepted a pact designed to ensure lasting fiscal restraint, Tietmeyer praised nations for agreeing to the pact and hailed the spirit of the weekend summit.
"The central importance of permanent fiscal discipline was recognised in Dublin," Tietmeyer told journalists when asked to comment on the outcome of last weekend's summit.

For Germany, and especially its Finance Minister Theo Waigel who conceived the stability pact last year, the agreement was celebrated as a great triumph to help assure Europeans that the new Euro will be a very stable currency.

For Tietmeyer, the acceptance of certain key elements in the pact designed to assure fiscal stability signalled that clear barriers have been erected to prevent European nations from running up excessive budget deficits.
"A three percent budget deficit (as a ratio to gross domestic product) has been set as an upper limit," he said.
More generally, he said "Without a doubt (the pact) is a paring back the national politicians' room to manoeuvre."
But Tietmeyer also stressed that the pact alone did not guarantee that Europe's new currency would be as stable as the mark.

The future of the monetary union to a large extent still depends on how these key elements will be applied, Tietmeyer added. "It is very important to see how these cornerstones will be made more concrete," he added.

Turning to an even more elementary step for the union, the decision on which nations would be allowed to enter, Tietmeyer said he was sure the Maastricht Treaty would be interpreted in the right spirit.

Evading tough questions on whether he believes nations who do not exactly meet the reference values on the budget and debt criteria will be allowed to join the union in 1999, Tietmeyer said only "The Commission will uphold the Maastricht Treaty."

He added the Treaty specified the reference values, giving a number for nations to aim for, but also had a verbal amendment, stating exceptional circumstances in which a nation may be eligible even if the numbers are not quite right.
The reference values are for a nation's budget deficit not to exceed three percent of GDP and debt not to exceed 60 pct.
The Bundesbank has talked a hard line, demanding a strict interpretation of these criteria, but Tietmeyer has also always stressed that the Treaty itself allows room for interpretation.
At present only Luxembourg out of the 15 European Union members would meet all the entry criteria for the union.
Tietmeyer also warned nations not to sit back and expect the European currency union to be able to solve the structural problems plaguing so many at the moment.
Unemployment and a host of other issues must be solved before nations enter the currency union, not afterwards, Tietmeyer warned.
"Preparation is more important than to wait for the currency union to solve a nation's structural problems," he said.
